title: The First Meeting — Interactive Scenario
audience: Social work students practising first-session communication
setting: Student Services, Monday morning, public secondary school, Western Australia

characters.You: School social worker (the learner; originally Sam in the source script)

source: Adapted from Initial Engagement - Jack.docx (user-provided). Main scenario follows the source; alternative dialogue branches are proposed teaching additions. Original source names the social worker Sam; the learner-facing version uses You.

context.setting: Student Services, Monday morning, at a public secondary school in Western Australia.
context.role: You are a school social worker. You have spent time supporting students in Jack’s classroom, but this is your first individual conversation with him.
context.student: Jack is 12 and in Year 7. He has recently moved from primary school to secondary school.
context.background: Jack’s close primary-school friends attend different schools, and he has found making new friends difficult. Ms Taylor has noticed that he sometimes seems distracted or disengaged in lessons, particularly when copying things off the board. He also appears uncomfortable in noisy, busy classrooms.
context.purpose: Ms Taylor has asked Jack to come to Student Services. Your aim is to get to know Jack, hear his perspective and explore how school has been going.

opening.text: Jack appears at the doorway with his school bag.
Hey, Jack! How are you?
Good.
How's your day going?
Alright.
Yeah? Come in, mate. Grab a seat wherever you like.
Jack puts his bag beside a chair and sits down.
How was your weekend? Do anything interesting?
Not really.
Just a quiet one?
Yeah. Played some games.
Oh, nice. What were you playing?
Minecraft.
Ah, Minecraft. Were you playing on your own or with someone?
With my cousin. But he kept dying.
(Laughs) Oh no. Was he any good?
Nah. He kept losing all our stuff.
Oh, that's annoying. Did you manage to get it back?
Some of it.
Fair enough. Sounds like you had a pretty good weekend then.
Yeah, I guess.
You settle back into the chair.
You've seen me in your classroom a few times, haven't you?
Yeah.
I think I was there last Thursday. In Ms Taylor's class?
Yeah.
Yeah, that's right. I come into different classes sometimes, help out a bit, talk to students. Have you been down to Student Services before?
Um, once. When I lost my timetable.
Oh, right. Did you find it in the end?
Nah, they printed me another one.
Ah, good. Easy fix.
Jack looks towards the door.

scene.text: So, did Ms Taylor tell you why she wanted you to come and see me today?
Not really. She just said I had to come here.

options.label: Explain the meeting and invite Jack’s agreement
options.sam: No, you’re not in trouble. Ms Taylor thought it might help to talk about how school’s going. I’d like to hear your side. Is that okay?

reaction.text: Oh. Okay. I thought I did something wrong.
I can see why you might have wondered that.
Yeah.

options.note: The purpose becomes clearer; Jack is invited to participate rather than treated as a problem.

options.label: Reassure without really explaining
options.sam: Nah, you’re all good, mate. Don’t worry. We’re just having a chat.

reaction.text: Okay…
Jack shifts in his chair and glances at the door.

options.note: Jack has heard reassurance, but the reason for the meeting remains uncertain.

options.label: Begin with the teacher’s concern
options.sam: Ms Taylor says you haven’t been finishing work in English. She wants me to find out why.

reaction.text: But I do my work!
Jack leans back and folds his arms.

options.note: Jack may experience this as another adult blaming him, even if Sam’s intention is to help.

options.label: Acknowledge the impact and reframe
options.sam: Sorry, Jack. I think I made it sound like you’ve done something wrong. That’s not what I meant. I’d like to hear what school has been like for you, from your point of view.

reaction.text: Oh. Okay.
Jack uncrosses his arms, although he still looks a little unsure.

options.label: Keep questioning his classroom behaviour
options.sam: So why aren’t you finishing the work?

reaction.text: I dunno.
Is there something making it difficult?
Can I just go back to class?

A.text: Sort of getting used to it. There’s heaps more people.
Science sometimes. We made circuits. But I don’t like English.
Oh yeah? What’s happening in English?
We have to copy heaps off the board. Everyone’s talking and sometimes I can’t finish before Miss changes it.
That sounds frustrating. Thanks for telling me.

B.text: What’s Year 7 been like for you?
Heaps more people. Different rooms all day.
I dunno. Sometimes there’s too much writing.
What happens when there’s too much?
I don’t always finish it. And it’s noisy.
That sounds frustrating. Thanks for telling me.

C_repaired.text: We don’t have to start with English. What’s Year 7 been like for you?
There’s heaps more people. I get lost sometimes.
There’s heaps to copy down. Sometimes I can’t keep up.

n2.title: Are you gonna tell Miss?

scene.text: A brief pause. Jack looks at you.

n2.prompt: How would you explain what can and cannot be kept private?

options.label: Explain confidentiality and its limits
options.sam: I won’t repeat everything you say. I keep brief notes, and I may need to share information if someone isn’t safe. If talking to a teacher could help, I’d discuss it with you first where possible. Does that make sense?

reaction.text: Yeah. I just don’t want her getting annoyed again.
I hear you. We can talk about what you’d feel okay with.

options.note: A realistic, age-appropriate account of information sharing; exact duties must be checked against local policy.

options.label: Give vague reassurance
options.sam: Nah, don’t worry about it. You’re fine.

reaction.text: But… would she find out?
Jack waits for a clearer answer.

options.note: The immediate concern remains unanswered. Jack may not feel able to decide what to disclose.

options.label: Promise complete secrecy
options.sam: No. I promise I won’t tell anyone what you’ve said.

reaction.text: Really? Okay.
Jack looks relieved and seems more willing to talk.

options.note: The reassurance may work in the short term, but it is an inaccurate promise and must be corrected.

options.label: Answer directly and check understanding
options.sam: Sorry, I didn’t really answer your question. I don’t repeat everything you tell me. I keep some notes, and sometimes I have to share something if someone isn’t safe. If talking with a teacher might help, I’d discuss that with you first where possible. How does that sound?

reaction.text: Okay. I just don’t want everyone knowing.
That makes sense. We can take this one step at a time.

options.label: Move on without answering
options.sam: Let’s not worry about it now. What do you do at lunchtime?

reaction.text: I don’t really want to talk about that.
Okay. We don’t have to.
Can I go back to class?

options.label: Correct the promise now
options.sam: Jack, I need to correct something I just said. I shouldn’t have promised I’d never tell anyone. Most of what you say stays between us, but if someone isn’t safe I may need to share information. I’d explain that to you as much as possible. I’m sorry I wasn’t clear.

reaction.text: So you might tell Miss?
Not automatically. We’d talk about what might be helpful to share, and with whom, unless there’s a safety reason I have to act.
Okay…

options.label: Leave the promise uncorrected
options.sam: So, what do you usually do at lunchtime?

reaction.text: Usually go to the library.
Jack continues, believing that nothing he says could ever be shared.

clear.text: What about lunchtime? Do you get a bit of a break from the noise then?
Yeah. Sometimes I go to the library. It’s quiet.
Do you hang out with anyone from your classes?
Sometimes these boys, but they’ve known each other since primary school.
Did anyone from your primary school come here?
Nah. My friends all went to different schools.
Doesn’t sound like lunchtime’s been much fun lately.
Have you mentioned any of this to anyone at school?

cautious.text: We don’t have to talk about anything you’re not ready for. What’s lunchtime usually like?
It’s okay. I go to the library.
What do you like about it?
It’s quiet. And I don’t really know many people here.
That sounds like quite a change from primary school.
Yeah. My friends went to other schools.
Have you wanted anyone at school to help with that?

misled.text: What about lunchtime? What’s that been like?
I mostly go to the library. I don’t really have friends here.
Yeah. My old friends all go to different schools. The boys here already know each other.
Have you talked with anyone at school about that?

n3.title: I don’t want them to make it a big thing.

scene.text: I don’t want them to make it a big thing.
Yeah, I hear you. You don’t want lots of people getting involved.

options.label: Ask Jack what support would feel manageable
options.sam: We don’t need to decide now. Would you rather talk again, or think about one small thing that might help? I’ll explain any steps I need to take.

reaction.text: Maybe I could just come here again. I don’t want Miss involved yet.
Okay. We can start by talking again. We’ll discuss any next steps together.

options.note: Jack helps define the next step; collaboration does not mean guaranteeing that nothing will ever need to be shared.

options.label: Arrange teacher involvement immediately
options.sam: I think Ms Taylor should know. I’ll speak with her so we can get some support in place.

reaction.text: No, please don’t! I said I don’t want that.
Jack grips the strap of his school bag.

options.note: A well-intended support plan is introduced without first exploring Jack’s preferences.

options.label: Accept that Jack is not ready to act
options.sam: Okay. We don’t need to sort anything out today. You’re welcome to talk again another time.

reaction.text: Okay. Maybe.
Jack looks relieved that he is not being pushed to decide.

options.note: A valid way to respect pace, provided Sam still attends to any safeguarding duties and leaves a route back to support.

options.label: Acknowledge the push and restore choice
options.sam: You’re right. I got ahead of myself. I’m sorry. I haven’t spoken to Ms Taylor about this conversation. Let’s talk about what you would and wouldn’t be comfortable with, and what I may need to do if there’s a safety concern.

reaction.text: I just don’t want everyone asking me questions.
That makes sense. Would you rather leave it for today or talk again another time?
Maybe another time.

options.label: Insist on the proposed plan
options.sam: I know you’re worried, but adults need to deal with this. I’ll talk to her.

reaction.text: Then I’m not saying anything else. Can I go?
Jack picks up his bag.

promise_reveal.title: But you said...

scene.text: But you said you wouldn’t tell anybody.
Jack remembers your earlier promise of complete secrecy. Even discussing possible support now creates confusion.

promise_reveal.prompt: What would you say to Jack?

options.label: Acknowledge and correct the promise
options.sam: You’re right, Jack. I did say that, and I was wrong to promise it. I’m sorry. I won’t repeat everything you’ve said, but there are safety situations where I may need to share information. Before we decide anything else, I want to make sure you understand that.

reaction.text: Oh. Okay. I need to think about it.
Of course. You don’t have to decide about next steps right now.

options.label: Deflect Jack’s concern
options.sam: Don’t worry about that. I’m just trying to help.

reaction.text: I want to go back to class.

collaborative.title: You agree to talk again

script.text: We’ve talked about English, lunchtime, and getting used to Year 7. We don’t need to cover everything today. Would another chat here be okay, or would you rather leave it for now?
I could come back another time.
Okay. We can plan that together.

collaborative.summary: Jack has had a meaningful say in what happens next. This is a promising initial connection, not a solved school problem.
reflect: Which explanations helped Jack make an informed choice?
How was Jack’s preference included in planning?

cautious.title: The conversation pauses

script.text: We don’t have to decide anything more today. If you want to talk again, we can. I’ll explain any steps I need to take.

cautious.summary: Jack is not ready to commit to support. Respecting his pace can still be appropriate trauma-informed practice.
reflect: What might Jack need before feeling ready to re-engage?
What responsibilities remain for you after this session?

early1.title: Jack returns to class

script.text: Okay. We don’t need to keep talking now. I’m sorry I made this feel like you were in trouble. You’re welcome to talk with me another time.
Jack takes his bag and returns to class.

early1.summary: The first conversation ends before Jack has discussed his school experiences. You should follow school safeguarding and follow-up procedures as appropriate.
reflect: How did the opening frame Jack as a problem?
How could you approach a future invitation differently?

early2.title: Jack chooses to leave

script.text: Okay. We can stop here. I’m sorry I wasn’t clear when you asked about telling Ms Taylor. Before you go, I can explain what I can keep private, if you’d like.

early2.summary: Jack leaves without further disclosure. An unanswered question about information sharing may have undermined his sense of safety.
reflect: What did Jack need to know to make an informed decision?
How could you keep the door open without pressure?

early3.title: The conversation ends early

script.text: Okay, we’ll stop talking for now. I can see this hasn’t felt okay to you.
Jack leaves. You must not treat his refusal as permission to ignore any actual safety concerns.

early3.summary: The proposed help was not negotiated with Jack. The relationship may need repair before future engagement.
reflect: How did the suggestion change the power dynamic?
Which smaller steps might have maintained Jack’s agency?

earlyPromise.title: Jack asks to leave

script.text: Okay. I won’t keep you here. I’m sorry I wasn’t clear about what can be kept private.
Jack leaves the session. You must clarify the misinformation appropriately and follow relevant practice procedures.

earlyPromise.summary: The earlier inaccurate promise has had a delayed consequence. Initial reassurance is not equivalent to informed trust.
reflect: Why did the inaccurate promise initially appear effective?
What would accountable repair require now?

notes.no_labels: Do not describe choices to learners as “correct/incorrect” during play. Pathway titles are for authoring only.
notes.no_scoring: Do not represent trust as a numeric score. Record choices and branch flags for story continuity.
notes.no_diagnosis: Do not imply Jack has a trauma diagnosis, ADHD, disability, abuse history, or mental-health condition.
notes.policy: Information-sharing scripts are examples, not a substitute for WA school child-protection/recordkeeping policy or site-specific supervision. Do not make unconditional secrecy promises.
notes.endings: Early endings are valid learner outcomes; student autonomy does not remove safety and statutory duties.
notes.educational: Jack’s reactions are one plausible narrative outcome, not certain psychological predictions.
notes.presentation: Show Context on its own screen. The opening conversation follows Start Conversation. Hide pedagogical option labels, TIP principle pills, decision counts, grading, pathway tracking and repair categories. Display the chosen dialogue and Jack’s reaction without explanatory feedback until What happened? and Reflection at an ending.
notes.display_order: Option IDs are internal stable keys for branching (A/B/C semantics from v1). display_order lists those keys in visual sequence; visible A/B/C letters are assigned by position, not by semantic ID.
